extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and scholars of English common law (readers of Blackstone)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the legal rules, qualifications, appointment methods, powers, duties, and limitations of subordinate magistrates in England (sheriffs, coroners, justices of the peace, bailiffs, gaolers, constables, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheriff — method of appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheriffs were formerly chosen by the inhabitants of the counties, but by statute and long usage the judges (originally twelve or all the judges) nominate three persons to the king, who appoints one; the king cannot now legally appoint otherwise than according to the known and established law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic progression: popular election → selection by chancellor/treasurer/chief justices (statutes cited) → customary meeting in exchequer (morrow of All Souls / St. Martin) where judges nominate three persons. Case law and reports discussed (e.g., Elizabeth appointing sheriffs during plague as exceptional). Emphasis that appointment must conform to statute and custom; 'non obstante' prerogative doctrine weakened by the Bill of Rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheriff — tenure and limits of service
rubrics_metrics.description: By old statutes sheriffs are to continue in office no longer than one year; nevertheless form of royal writ may be 'durante bene placito' (during the king's pleasure); statute 1 Anne st. 1. c. 8 allows officers to hold six months after the king's demise unless displaced; statute 1 Ric. II. c. 11 prevents compulsion to serve sheriff again within three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences: office normally annual; temporary exceptions (durante bene placito, death/demise of king); statutory protections against immediate reappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheriff — judicial jurisdiction (small civil causes & electoral returns)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a judge the sheriff is to hear and determine all causes of forty shillings value and under in his county court; he also has judicial power in various other civil causes and decides elections of knights of the shire, coroners, and verderors, judging voter qualifications and returning those he determines duly elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited civil jurisdiction explicitly quantified (40s). Electoral functions subject to control of the House of Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheriff — role as keeper of the king's peace (powers and statutory limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheriff, both by common law and by special commission, is the principal conservator of the peace in the county: he may apprehend and commit persons breaking the peace, bind persons in recognizances, pursue traitors/felons, command the posse comitatus, and summon persons over fifteen (not peers) to attend on warning; but by Magna Carta and statute law he and certain officers are forbidden to hold pleas of the crown or try criminal offences and may not act as an ordinary justice of the peace while sheriff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power includes arrest/commitment and posse comitatus (summons of all persons >15 to assist). Explicit limit: forbidden to try criminal cases (avoids being both judge and executioner) and cannot act as ordinary justice of peace concurrently (statutes cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheriff — ministerial duties to the courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheriff is bound to execute all process issuing from the king's courts: serve writs, arrest, take bail, summon and return juries, and carry judgments into execution (including capital sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties span all stages: commencement (serve writ), trial (summon/return jury), post-judgment (execution). Emphasizes ministerial (not discretionary) nature of these duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheriff — duties as the king's bailiff (royal fiscal and custody functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the king's bailiff the sheriff must seize lands devolved to the crown by attainder or escheat, levy fines and forfeitures, seize and keep waifs, wrecks, estrays (unless granted), and collect the king's rents within his bailiwick if commanded by process from the Exchequer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role preserves royal rights within the county; many duties touch on revenue and property for the crown (statutory and common-law bases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on sheriff's subordinate officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Under-sheriff, bailiffs, and gaolers must not buy, sell, or farm their offices (forfeiture of 500_l. cited); no under-sheriff shall hold office above one year (statute 42 Edw. III. c. 9) and under-sheriffs or sheriff's officers shall not practice as attorneys (stat. 1 Hen. V. c. 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: avoid partiality, oppression, and corruption. Noted abuses: evasion by nominal deputies and practising through others; statutory penalties for breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bailiffs — types and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Bailiffs are either bailiffs of hundreds (appointed by sheriffs to collect fines, summon juries, attend judges at assizes and quarter sessions, execute writs in the hundreds) or special bailiffs (skilled persons employed for serving writs, arrests, and executions); sheriff is answerable for their misdemeanors and they are usually bound in bond (bound-bailiffs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes routine local bailiffs from 'special' expert bailiffs used for arrests/executions; bond used as security for due execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaolers — duties and sheriff's liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaolers (prison-keepers) must keep safely all persons committed by lawful warrant; if prisoners escape, the sheriff answers to the king for criminal matters or to the injured party in civil matters; the sheriff must have lands sufficient to answer the king and his people; abuses restrained by statute 32 Geo. II. c. 28.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes responsibility and financial liability of sheriff for custody failures; statutory protections of prisoners and limits on gaoler abuses noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of sheriff's ceremonial expense and retinue
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute 13 & 14 Car. II. c. 21 restricts sheriffs from keeping any table at assizes except for their family, giving presents to judges or their servants, or having more than forty men in livery; minimum numbers for decency/safety: not less than twenty men in England and twelve in Wales; forfeiture for breach 200_l.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: prevent excessive private expenditure/burdens on the subject while preserving minimal public decorum and security at assizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coroner — origin, title, and election
rubrics_metrics.description: The coroner is an ancient common-law officer (coronator) concerned with pleas of the crown; coroners are chosen by freeholders in the county court (writ de coronatore eligendo), with statutes (Westm. I) requiring election of 'lawful and discreet knights' and wording directing the sheriff to choose 'such as will better and know, and will and can, intend that office to him'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Election by freeholders preserves ancient democratic trace; statutory prescription of qualification and the writ's specific command demonstrates the public character and dignity of the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coroner — qualifications and requisite estate
rubrics_metrics.description: A coroner ought to have an estate sufficient to maintain the dignity of the office and to answer any fines for misbehaviour; if not enough, the fine shall be levied on the county (punishment for electing an insufficient officer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory and common-law insistence on social/financial status to ensure probity and that fines are collectible; historical complaints about decline in quality and the allowance of fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coroner — tenure and grounds for removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Coroners are chosen for life but may be removed by being made sheriff or verderor (incompatibility), or by king's writ de coronatore exonerando for assigned causes (engaged in other business, incapacitated by age or sickness, insufficient estate, inconvenient residence); statute 25 Geo. II. c. 29 adds extortion, neglect, or misbehaviour as causes for removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies both structural incompatibilities and misconduct/ incapacity as removal grounds; statutory modernization (25 Geo. II) expands removable causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coroner — judicial duties and procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary duty is to inquire when a person is slain or dies suddenly, and this must be 'super visum corporis' (upon view of the body); the coroner must sit at the place of death, empanel a jury from neighbouring towns (4–6), commit those found guilty to prison, inquire into deodands, certify the inquisition to king's bench or next assizes, and also enquire concerning shipwrecks, wrecks, and treasure trove (including identity of finders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict procedures: body must be found for coroner to sit; local jury composition and place-of-death requirement are procedural safeguards; duties also include property-related inquiries (deodands, treasure, wreck).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coroner — ministerial (substitute) role vis-à-vis sheriff
rubrics_metrics.description: When just exception can be taken to the sheriff for suspicion of partiality (e.g., interest in the suit or kinship to a party), process must be awarded to the coroner instead of the sheriff for execution of the king's writs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coroner serves as an impartial substitute to avoid sheriff-related conflicts of interest in executing royal process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservators of the peace — who they are and their powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The king is the principal conservator of the peace; general conservators include the lord chancellor/keeper, lord treasurer, lord high steward, lord marshal, lord high constable, all justices of King's Bench, and master of the rolls; they may commit breakers of the peace or bind them in recognizances. Coroners, sheriffs, constables, and tythingmen are conservators within their jurisdictions and may apprehend breakers and bind in sureties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conservatorship is tied to office and jurisdiction; power to commit or take recognizances is central to maintaining the king's peace. Local officers' powers are limited to their jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justices of the peace — origin and appointment by commission
rubrics_metrics.description: Justices of the peace (formerly conservators) are appointed by the king's special commission under the Great Seal; the form (settled A.D. 1590) appoints them jointly and severally to keep the peace, and contains a 'quorum' clause naming particular justices one of whom must be present for certain business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key formalities: royal commission under Great Seal, 'quorum' clause (certain named justices of the quorum must be present), and historic statutory fixation of the commission's form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justices of the peace — number and statutory qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes required initially small numbers (e.g., two or three of best reputation — 18 Edw. III. c.2; one lord and three/four of most worthy — 34 Edw. III. c.1; later restrictions to six/eight), residence in county (2 Hen. V), sufficient estate (e.g., 20_l. per annum — 18 Hen. VI), and to be of best reputation, the most worthy men, some learned in law; later growth in number due to increased statutory duties and a statute (5 Geo. II. c.11) adjusting property qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifications combine moral reputation, property/residence and legal learning; statutory amounts change with time (historic figures cited) and the modern practice expanded commissions due to statutory workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justices of the peace — powers to enquire and try offences
rubrics_metrics.description: The commission empowers justices collectively (any two or more) to enquire of and determine felonies and other misdemeanors and to keep the peace; statute 34 Edw. III. c. 1 gave them power of trying felonies (hence the title 'justices').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational rule: business may be transacted by any two or more justices (subject to 'quorum' exceptions naming particular justices). Their authority extends from conservatorship to judicial functions for criminal matters as statute-law expanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical change in election/assignment of conservators of the peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally conservators of the peace were chosen by freeholders in county court; after political crisis in Edward II/Isabel/Edward III era the election was taken from the people and given to the king (assignment by king's commission) to maintain public order, and the office evolved (statutes cited) into modern justices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the constitutional/political rationale for transfer of appointment power from populace to Crown (prevent disorder) and statutory developments giving justices greater jurisdiction (e.g., the power to try felonies).
